Where mining and reclamation extends to where the coal cropped out along the valleys, the rate of spring discharge will probably be somewhat higher than the natural rate of spring discharge. When a buffer zone of unmined rock separates the reclaimed aquifer from the natural valleys, spring discharge if any will probably be reduced.
The post-reclamation spring discharge along the west side of Tract III is not expected to be much different than from premining conditions. This is because the natural rate of spring discharge is very low and is from local precipitation and infiltration from very near the outcrop. Spring discharge to the valley of East Fork Sarpy Creek from Tract III is expected to be greater where the reclaimed aquifer crops out along the valley. The discharge will be at a somewhat lesser rate where a buffer zone of unmined rock occurs between the valley and the excavation. In this valley, however, most of the natural ground-water discharge disappears into the alluvium of the East Fork of Sarpy Creek and does not appreciably contribute to the surface stream flow, especially during low flow periods.
On Tract II the lateral flow of ground-water to the Robinson Coal and younger rocks from the highland areas to the south is very minimal, due to the deep incision of streams, and ground-water is recharged almost entirely from local precipitation. The zone of saturation is much thinner than on Tract III. Because the bedrock units dip to the northeast, most of the ground-water flow is in that direction. The ground-water discharge from Tract II is, on an annual basis, essentially equivalent to the infiltration from precipitation.
